title: How should facilities teams coordinate office lunch catering?
body_markdown:
Facilities teams should coordinate office lunch catering through one shared brief covering attendance, dietary requirements, building access, service arrangements and clearance. Assign a named owner to each task, agree the caterer’s responsibilities in writing, and confirm changes through one contact. This facilities team office lunch catering checklist separates what the caterer provides from what your office must arrange, so neither side relies on assumptions.


**TL;DR**

- Use a facilities team office lunch catering checklist to assign access, dietary requirements, service and clearance responsibilities.
- myCHEF provides corporate catering; confirm the proposed menu, staffing and practical arrangements before agreeing the brief.
- Choose boxed meals for individual distribution, a buffet for shared service, or staffed catering when service support matters.
- Confirm the final attendance count and change deadline with the caterer, rather than relying on calendar invitations.


## How should facilities teams coordinate office lunch catering?

**Give one facilities contact ownership of the delivery-to-clearance plan, while the event organiser owns attendance and purchasing approval.** The caterer should receive a single agreed brief, not separate instructions from reception, finance and the person choosing the menu.

For menu and service-format context, the guide to [corporate lunch catering in Dubai](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/best-corporate-lunch-catering-companies-in-dubai) is a useful companion. Use this checklist to settle the operational responsibilities before requesting a proposal.

Follow this sequence:

1. **Attendance:** confirm who is eating, where they will eat and whether lunch happens together or in separate breaks.
2. **Dietary brief:** collect meal preferences and allergy information, then ask the caterer to confirm what they can accommodate.
3. **Building access:** agree the arrival route, reception contact, unloading arrangements and access permissions.
4. **Service setup:** choose the distribution format and identify the required space, equipment and people.
5. **Meal handover:** name the person accepting delivery and checking meals against the agreed order.
6. **Clearance:** agree who collects equipment, removes packaging and returns the area to normal use.

Keep these details together. A menu approval is not an access approval, and a delivery confirmation is not confirmation that serving staff will attend.


![Office lunch coordination sequence from attendance and dietary requirements through delivery and clearance](https://gwvckixiegkllthleuyt.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/workspace-article-images-public/cd6da06c-43c4-4da5-8218-7bf53c2f33b9/body-656a49c3ae113809d1ecc2c1c3f06f42.jpg)

*Confirm the complete lunch operation, not just the menu.*


## Why does a shared catering brief matter?

Office lunch involves responsibilities that sit across different teams. Facilities understands the building, the organiser knows the guests, procurement controls the order, and the caterer needs clear instructions about food and service.

A shared brief gives everyone the same reference point. It also makes exclusions visible: if no one has agreed to provide serving utensils, replenish a buffet or remove hired equipment, those jobs remain unresolved.

**Treat lunch as a short workplace operation with an owner, a handover and a finish.** That approach works for an internal meeting, a client presentation or a larger company gathering without turning every meal into an elaborate event.

## Who should own each part of the lunch?

Allocate responsibilities before discussing menu details. One person can hold several roles, but each task still needs an explicit owner and a way to reach them.

| Responsibility | Suggested owner | Confirmation needed |
|---|---|---|
| Attendance and meal count | Event organiser | Final count, visitors and separate lunch groups |
| Dietary information | Event organiser or nominated coordinator | Requirements communicated to the caterer |
| Purchase approval | Budget holder or procurement | Approved scope and ordering process |
| Building access | Facilities or building contact | Entry route, permissions and unloading arrangements |
| Delivery acceptance | Named on-site contact | Meeting point and order-checking responsibility |
| Food setup and service | Caterer or office team, as agreed | Equipment, staffing and exact division of work |
| Clearance and collection | Facilities and caterer, as agreed | Waste, hired items and collection arrangements |

The event organiser should send consolidated changes to the facilities contact. The facilities contact should then communicate operational changes to the caterer, rather than asking the supplier to reconcile conflicting messages.

Give reception the delivery contact and destination. Do not make reception responsible for checking dietary meals or approving substitutions unless that responsibility has been expressly assigned.

## Which office lunch format should you choose?

Choose the format around your office’s ability to receive, distribute and clear the food. The menu comes next.

The following are planning options to discuss with a caterer, not a statement that every supplier includes each format or service.

| Format | Best for | Practical advantage | Trade-off to resolve |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individually boxed meals | Desk lunches or separate breaks | Individual distribution without a shared serving station | Packaging removal and clear identification of meal variants |
| Drop-off buffet | Teams eating together in a suitable shared area | Guests can choose from the agreed dishes | Your team needs ownership of setup, replenishment and clearance unless included |
| Staffed lunch service | Hosted lunches where service support matters | Agreed staff can manage the serving area | Staffing scope, workspace and equipment need separate confirmation |

### Individually boxed meals

**Choose boxed meals when individual distribution matters more than a shared dining experience.** Ask how meal variants will be identified and how the delivery will be grouped for departments or separate lunch areas.

The main limitation is what happens after handover. Your office still needs a distribution plan, a place for meals awaiting collection and a packaging-clearance arrangement.

### Drop-off buffet

**Choose a drop-off buffet when you have a suitable serving area and someone to manage it.** Confirm whether the proposal includes setup, serving equipment and collection, rather than assuming that delivery covers them.

A buffet gives guests choice, but it also requires an orderly route through the serving area. Decide who will answer menu questions and contact the caterer if the delivered order needs checking.

### Staffed lunch service

**Choose staffed service when you need agreed on-site support, not simply more food.** Ask which tasks the staff will perform: setting up, serving, replenishing, clearing tables or collecting equipment.

Staffing does not remove the need for facilities coordination. Staff still need access, a working area and a clear handover with the office contact.

## What should facilities check before the caterer arrives?

Walk the delivery route as someone unfamiliar with the office would use it. Start at the building entrance and finish at the actual serving area, not at reception.

For a Dubai office, ask your building contact about loading access, visitor registration, security instructions and use of service lifts. Confirm the rules for your premises rather than assuming another building’s arrangements apply.

Your access checklist should cover:

- **Arrival point:** the entrance or loading area the delivery team should use.
- **Security process:** any information or permissions your building requires.
- **Internal route:** the floor, lift and room the team needs to reach.
- **Delivery contact:** a person who can answer the phone and meet the team.
- **Serving area:** a cleared surface or room that does not obstruct normal movement.
- **Equipment needs:** anything the proposed service requires, with supply responsibilities agreed.
- **Collection route:** how equipment and packaging will leave after lunch.

Tell the caterer whether your office has food-preparation facilities, refrigeration or only a basic pantry. Ask what the proposed menu requires; do not assume an office kitchen can support finishing or holding every dish.

If the space is shared with other businesses, the guide to [catering for co-working spaces in Dubai](https://www.mychef.ae/blog/catering-for-co-working-spaces-in-dubai-complete-guide) addresses the related setting. Your own brief should still identify which areas you control and which require permission.

## How should you handle dietary requirements and allergies?

Ask guests to distinguish preferences from allergies or other requirements that need specific confirmation. Give the caterer the information needed to assess the request without circulating unnecessary personal details throughout the office.

**A dietary request is not confirmed until the caterer has accepted it for the proposed menu and service.** Ask how meals will be identified, how service staff will recognise them, and what guests should do if they have a question.

For allergies, request clear information about ingredients and preparation arrangements. Do not describe a meal as allergen-free or suitable for a particular guest unless the caterer has explicitly confirmed that claim.

Agree how substitutions will be handled. If a dish changes after approval, the organiser needs updated dietary information before distributing it; the original menu description is no longer enough.

## What should the catering proposal include and exclude?

Ask for a written scope that separates food, delivery, equipment, staffing and clearance. This makes proposals easier to compare without reducing the decision to the menu alone.

For myCHEF corporate catering, businesses should confirm the menu and operational scope against their event brief. **myCHEF is best suited to businesses seeking corporate event catering rather than recurring household cooking.** Building access and responsibilities remain items to agree for the specific booking.

Check the proposal against this list:

- The menu, meal quantities and agreed dietary variants.
- The delivery location and agreed arrival arrangements.
- Whether food arrives ready for distribution or needs setup.
- Whether serving utensils, crockery, cutlery and other equipment are included.
- Whether staff attend and which duties they perform.
- Who handles leftovers, packaging, waste and equipment collection.
- The process for changes, substitutions and cancellations.

Avoid vague scope descriptions such as everything included. Ask what happens in practice, from arrival to departure, and record the answer.

## Why does the office lunch scope vary?

The right arrangement depends on the workplace and the event. Use these factors to explain differences between proposals, rather than assuming the same meal count requires the same service:

- **Attendance pattern:** one shared lunch and separate departmental breaks need different distribution plans.
- **Dietary requirements:** confirmed variants affect menu planning and meal identification.
- **Service format:** individual meals, buffet service and staffed service require different handovers.
- **Building access:** unloading and the internal delivery route shape arrival arrangements.
- **Available facilities:** pantry space and equipment determine what the office can support.
- **Clearance responsibilities:** supplier collection and office-managed cleanup are different scopes.

When comparing proposals, send each caterer the same brief. Otherwise, you are comparing different assumptions rather than different responses to the same requirement.

## What should happen on the day of the lunch?

The on-site contact should be ready to meet the delivery team and check the order. Keep the agreed brief accessible so that the check uses confirmed details, not someone’s recollection of the menu.

Check the meal count, dietary variants, equipment and serving location before accepting the handover as complete. If something differs, contact the caterer and organiser before distributing the affected meals.

Record operational problems factually: an unclear meeting point, missing utensils or an unassigned collection task. That gives the next booking a useful correction rather than a general complaint.

After lunch, confirm equipment collection and clearance. The job is finished when the area is ready for normal office use, not when the final guest has eaten.

## How do you keep recurring office lunches consistent?

Use the previous brief as a template, not as automatic approval for the next lunch. Reconfirm attendance, dietary requirements, menu, access and responsibilities for each occasion.

Keep a short record of changes that improved the operation. A clearer delivery entrance or a different serving position is useful information; an old attendance count is not a reliable ordering instruction.

For repeat corporate catering enquiries with myCHEF, explain the workplace pattern and the service you need. Ask which arrangements can be agreed for that scope rather than assuming recurring delivery, staffing or equipment is included.

## FAQ


**What should a facilities team office lunch catering checklist include?**

A facilities team office lunch catering checklist should include attendance, dietary requirements, building access, service setup, meal handover and clearance. Assign an owner to each task and confirm the caterer’s responsibilities in writing.

**Who should coordinate office lunch catering?**

One named facilities contact should coordinate delivery and site arrangements, while the organiser owns attendance and purchasing approval. Send the caterer one consolidated brief rather than separate departmental instructions.

**Is drop-off catering better than staffed catering for an office lunch?**

Drop-off catering suits an office that can manage the agreed setup, distribution and clearance itself. Staffed catering suits a lunch that needs defined on-site service support; confirm the duties included.

**How do we confirm the right number of lunches?**

Confirm the meal count with the organiser using expected diners, visitors and separate lunch groups. Agree a final-count deadline with the caterer instead of treating calendar invitations as confirmed attendance.

**How should we tell the caterer about food allergies?**

Give the caterer clear allergy information and ask them to confirm whether the proposed meal is suitable. Also agree meal identification and substitution procedures; a menu label alone does not establish suitability.

**What should we ask about delivery to a Dubai office?**

Ask about the arrival point, security process, unloading route, lift access and on-site contact. Confirm your building’s requirements with its management rather than assuming a standard process.

**Does office catering include cleaning up afterwards?**

Office catering includes cleanup only when that responsibility is agreed in the scope. Specify who removes packaging, clears the serving area and collects equipment.

**What information should we send with an office catering enquiry?**

Send the date, location, guest count and service required, together with dietary requirements and building-access details. Explain whether you need delivery only, setup or staffed service so the proposal addresses the actual lunch operation.

## Finish the brief with the clearance plan

**Before approving the lunch, ask who owns the room after service ends.** That question exposes unresolved responsibilities for packaging, serving equipment and collection while there is still time to agree them.

For a tailored myCHEF corporate catering enquiry, send the date, office location, guest count and service required. Include dietary requirements, building-access instructions and whether you need delivery, setup or staffed service. A clear brief lets the proposed menu and practical arrangements answer the same question: what does your office need for this lunch?
